To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

(i) frictional ageing at the nanoscale results from chemical bonds that form between contacting surfaces, (ii) the evolution of friction with time is the result of the growth of the number of bonds between contacting surfaces, and (iii) the evolution effect is much more significant at the nanoscal than at the macroscopic scale, and this difference can explain the evolution effect observed in laboratory experiments.

A comprehensive summary for our work would be that
we have shown that frictional ageing is the result of interfacial bond formation, and this mechanism is responsible for the evolution effect in rock friction.
the evolution effect is a manifestation of interfacial bonding, which is the result of the formation of chemical bonds between contacting surfaces.
the frictional ageing is not due to the contact area growth, but the chemical bonding between the contacting surfaces, which has important implications for earthquake physics.
The main takeaway from our work is that
frictional strengthening at the nanoscale arises from chemical bonding at the interface and not from asperity creep.
frictional ageing is a consequence of chemical reactions at the nanometrescale.
the time-dependent increase of static friction, or frictional ‘ageing’, is a result of chemical bonding at the interface, rather than changes in the area of contact.
